name: Bebop
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize/deserialize latency of tiny/simple/complex POCOs (once and in bulk), comparing Bebop (Message and Struct variants) against Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json, Google.Protobuf, and MessagePack-CSharp, in an independent third-party benchmark repo.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize complex POCO once: BebopStruct 166.1 ns vs Protobuf 1,051.4 ns (~6.3x faster) and vs MessagePack 1,584.6 ns (~9.5x faster); BebopMessage 231.7 ns similarly ~4.5x faster than Protobuf. Repo README states Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization' among the tested formats, and Protobuf becomes 'the slowest of the binary serializers' on deserialization.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.13.1, .NET SDK 6.0.100-preview.7.21379.14, .NET 5.0.9 (X64 RyuJIT)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 1 CPU, 32 logical / 16 physical cores, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Bebop also targets TypeScript, Rust, Dart, C, and other languages via its own IDL/codegen, but the cited numeric evidence here is specifically for its C# implementation. Requires a `.bop` schema and code generation step (like Protobuf), unlike schema-less formats.
caveats: The independent benchmark repo (ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks) is small (6 stars) and was last updated in 2021, so it predates recent Bebop/Protobuf/.NET releases; results may not reflect current versions. It is however a genuinely third-party, non-Bebop-affiliated benchmark with full BenchmarkDotNet environment info published, and Bebop's own docs/HN discussion corroborate a large speed advantage over Protobuf.

claimed_speedup: No claim by the project; numbers come from the third-party GLD.SerializerBenchmark C results (run 2026-09-29-182101, default paired-IQR k=1.5 statistics, mean ns). Ratios are derived from page data. Round trip at 100 instances, libbson ns vs cJSON ns: message 157,288 vs 338,948 (libbson 2.15x faster), document 546,018 vs 855,914 (1.57x), event 324,854 vs 502,001 (1.55x), telemetry 962,634 vs 3,078,221 (3.2x), but strings 1,168,630 vs 669,472 (cJSON 1.75x faster). Against jansson libbson is 1.97x to 3.28x faster on the same four payloads and equal on strings (1,168,630 vs 1,165,048); against json-c 2.13x to 2.81x faster on four payloads and 1.44x slower on strings; against parson 2.25x to 3.94x faster on four payloads and 1.52x slower on strings. Against yyjson libbson is slower on four of five payloads (document 546,018 vs 407,197; telemetry 962,634 vs 357,412) and only 1.06x faster on message. Against binary formats it is slower everywhere: mpack is 2.0x to 8.5x faster (document 191,878 ns) and libcbor-stream 1.4x to 5.5x faster.

name: libcbor
workload: Per-operation mean serialize + deserialize time (ns) of five fixed payload types (message, document, telemetry, strings, event) written to and read back from CBOR by a shared C harness, at 100 instances per payload (about 12 to 35 KB of CBOR) and at 1 instance (a few hundred bytes); libcbor's streaming cbor_encode_* encoder and its cbor_load DOM decoder against tinycbor's CborEncoder and CborValue cursor API.
claimed_speedup: No claim by the project; numbers come from the third-party GLD.SerializerBenchmark C results (run 2026-09-29-182101, default paired-IQR k=1.5 statistics, mean ns). Ratios are derived from page data. Round trip at 100 instances, tinycbor ns vs libcbor streaming-encode row ('libcbor-stream', encode via cbor_encode_*, decode via cbor_load): strings 1,018,100 vs 230,699 (4.4x faster), telemetry 680,871 vs 174,795 (3.9x), document 666,168 vs 322,178 (2.1x), message 195,514 vs 109,258 (1.8x), event 269,957 vs 185,809 (1.45x). Encode only, libcbor streaming encoder vs tinycbor encoder: document 47,333 vs 71,654 (1.5x), telemetry 23,161 vs 37,184 (1.6x), event 27,542 vs 40,213 (1.5x), message 12,315 vs 17,360 (1.4x), strings 39,841 vs 48,903 (1.2x). Decode, cbor_load plus DOM lookups vs tinycbor cursor decode: 1.45x (event) to 5.1x (strings). Plain 'libcbor' DOM row (cbor_item_t build, then cbor_load): round trip faster than tinycbor on 4 of 5 payloads (strings 3.0x, telemetry 2.75x, document 1.2x, message 1.2x) but slower on event (300,741 vs 269,957 ns, tinycbor 1.11x faster); DOM construction alone is 2x to 4x slower than tinycbor's encoder (document 277,071 vs 71,654 ns). At 1 instance the libcbor-stream rows are also faster on all five payloads (round trip document 4,314 vs 7,729 ns, strings 2,395 vs 10,542 ns), while the plain DOM row is within 1% on message (2,411 vs 2,424 ns) and slower on event (4,101 vs 3,495 ns).
compiler_and_flags: gcc (Ubuntu 11.4.0-1ubuntu1~22.04.3) 11.4.0; harness c/CMakeLists.txt defaults to Release with add_compile_options(-O2 -Wall); libcbor v0.11.0 built by CMake Release via c/scripts/fetch-and-build-deps.sh; tinycbor v0.6.0 compiled with cc -O2 (symbol-prefixed tc_).
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12800H (20 logical cores, up to 4700 MHz, governor powersave), 32 GB RAM, Linux 6.8.0-138-generic x86_64 (environment block of the result file; git state of the run marked dirty).
stars_or_usage: 405 stars; used by Yubico libfido2, Amazon AWS C SDK, QEMU (per repo README)
tradeoffs: libcbor builds a reference-counted cbor_item_t tree (one allocation per item unless cbor_set_allocs is pointed at an arena) and is the more complete CBOR implementation with streaming and incremental decoding; the speed here comes from its low-level cbor_encode_* functions, which write straight into a caller buffer, and from O(1) random access into decoded arrays. tinycbor allocates nothing and has a smaller footprint but is a forward-only cursor API.
caveats: Not a project claim and not a pure parser throughput test: the harness wrappers decide the access pattern. The libcbor rows install a 16 MiB bump-arena allocator through cbor_set_allocs (reset every op), which the wrapper calls the documented amortization pattern. The tinycbor decode wrapper locates every key with cbor_value_map_find_value (linear scan) and reaches array element i by advancing i times, so its decode time grows quadratically with array length; most of the 4x to 5x decode gaps on strings and telemetry come from that access pattern, not from raw parsing speed. The fairest numbers are the encode-only ones (1.2x to 1.6x) and the single-instance rows. The plain DOM row is slower than tinycbor at serialization and on the event payload. Results were measured on libcbor v0.11.0, before master's PR #434 (inline cbor_incref and cbor_decref, said by its author to give about 1.3x to 1.5x on the DOM path). The benchmark's maintainer filed libcbor issues #433 (call-path review request, open) and #440/#441 (spec compliance misses, closed Sep 16 2026), so the suite's own compliance matrix lists libcbor misses. The result file is a dashboard snapshot (dashboard/public/data/c_latest.json.gz); the interactive dashboard on github.io is blocked here and was not opened. Host used the powersave governor and a dirty git tree; about 85 to 96 kept samples per row after IQR filtering. libcbor's own README and docs have no benchmark.

name: Enchantum
baseline: magic_enum (compile-time enum reflection to string); simple_enum and conjure_enum also compared
workload: Generated translation units (benchmarks/gen.py) declaring 32 to 200 enum class types with 16 to 200 members each and calling to_string once per enum through a volatile; compile time averaged over 10 runs, plus object and executable size on Clang.

Default out-of-bounds checking (numbers in parentheses): Small 8.2 vs 47 s (5.7x, derived), Big 3.3 vs 21 s (6.4x, derived). Clang Small 5.8 vs 47 s; MSVC Small 15.8 (37.4) vs 80 s. Clang object size Small 275 KB vs magic_enum 732 KB (2.7x, derived), Big 84 vs 1307 KB (15.6x, derived); executable Small 40 vs 95 KB. Author's own project full rebuild 2 min to 1 min 26 s after switching from magic_enum.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.0 and Clang 20.1.2 with -O3, MSVC 19.44 (VS 2022) with /Ox; 10 runs averaged; exact command lines not stated. Test files generated by benchmarks/gen.py (magic_enum range set via MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE_MIN/MAX, enchantum via ENCHANTUM_MIN_RANGE/MAX_RANGE, conjure_enum with FIX8_CONJURE_ENUM_MINIMAL).
hardware: Windows 10 machine, CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: C++17 header-only enum reflection without macros; reflects values inside a configurable range (ENCHANTUM_MIN_RANGE/MAX_RANGE) like magic_enum; README lists no support for wide strings and points to docs/limitations.md. The default setting adds an out-of-bounds check (ENCHANTUM_CHECK_OUT_OF_BOUNDS_BY=2) that detects enums not fully reflected, at extra compile time.
caveats: First-party benchmark; CPU model missing, so it falls short of tier A, although the generator (benchmarks/gen.py) is public and its test-case parameters match the README table. The bold headline numbers appear to be with the out-of-bounds check disabled; the README says the parenthesised values are with the default setting (about 1.2x to 2.1x slower on GCC, and MSVC Small 37.4 vs 15.8 s), so the default-configuration win over magic_enum is smaller (for example 5.7x rather than 7.8x on GCC Small). simple_enum is faster on the Ideal Range case (2.7 vs 3 s on GCC); magic_enum is given the same ranges as enchantum (up to -1024..1024, where it timed out), and the Ideal Range case (0..50), where magic_enum is only 2.7x slower, is the least range-inflated comparison. No comparison with a hand-written switch or std::string_view table, and no runtime lookup benchmark. The Reddit post by a friend of the author linked from the README (cost of enum to string, C++26 reflection vs the old ways) was not reachable; no independent reproduction found.

name: Magic Enum
baseline: conjure_enum (fix8mt/conjure_enum), another macro-free C++ enum-reflection library
workload: Compile time of translation units reflecting 200 small enums (16 members, range -128..128), 32 big enums (200 members, range -256..256) and 100 enums with an ideal range (0..50), each averaged over 10 runs, plus object-file size on Clang.

Clang object size KB: Small 732 vs 779, Big 1307 vs 1400, Ideal 1051 vs 1123. The Large Range case (-1024..1024) timed out (>20 min) for magic_enum on GCC and MSVC.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 for GCC and Clang, /Ox for MSVC; compiler versions not stated; conjure_enum built with FIX8_CONJURE_ENUM_MINIMAL; magic_enum range set through MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE_MAX. Generator script: benchmarks/gen.py in ZXShady/enchantum.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 (GCC 9+, Clang 5+, MSVC 15.3+). Uses __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ probing over a bounded value range (MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE_MIN/MAX, default -128..128), so enums with larger values need per-enum customization; compile time grows with the range. Not a runtime-speed claim.

Its purpose is to show enchantum beats magic_enum: enchantum compiles 2.7x to 8.1x faster than magic_enum in the same table (for example GCC Small 6.0 s vs 47 s), simple_enum compiles faster than magic_enum in every row (GCC Small 21.5 s vs 47 s), and magic_enum's own object and executable sizes are 2.4x to 15.6x larger than enchantum's. The win over conjure_enum is implicit (the README lists conjure_enum as slow to compile with bigger binaries), conjure_enum is a niche baseline, and magic_enum is better read as the incumbent that others beat. Neither compiler versions nor CPU are stated, so this is first-party-to-a-rival, tier C. No runtime benchmark exists for magic_enum against std::string_view tables, switch statements or hand-written conversions: the repo has no benchmark directory, issue #40 has no numbers, and the Boost list thread and dev.to post that might have numbers are blocked here. Magic Enum's own README claims no speed numbers.

Read from the gh-pages index.html on raw.githubusercontent.com (the live github.io page is blocked here). The report averages wide and deep shapes per size, recomputes throughput from averaged sizes, and its throughput_mbs fields are inconsistent (libxml2 1MB shows 4913 MB/s), so only time_ms is quoted. Expat times are non-monotonic (100KB 4.59 ms vs 10MB 69 ms), which suggests the deep/narrow files or per-parse overhead dominate the small sizes. The libxml2 harness passes a zeroed xmlSAXHandler with only startElement, endElement and characters set (SAX1 mode, no default SAX2 tree-building callbacks, no entity or namespace work); the Expat harness creates and frees a parser per iteration; both discard the data. A 2.1x to 7.8x SAX gap in favour of libxml2 is far larger than older reports and was not cross-checked by running it. Conflicting snippet-only evidence from search results (mail.gnome.org, python.org expat-discuss, OSM dev list and PHP docs were blocked and not opened): one developer reported libxml2 about 30% faster than Expat, another reported Expat about 10% faster on OSM files, and PHP docs call libxml2 'slightly slower for SAX'. name: xmloxide
workload: Criterion benchmarks parsing, serializing, and XPath-querying an Atom feed, SVG drawing, Maven POM, XHTML page, and a 374KB XML document, comparing MiB/s and relative speedups against libxml2
claimed_speedup: Parsing roughly parity to slightly slower than libxml2 (176 vs 184 MiB/s on Atom feed, ~4% slower; 103 vs 92 MiB/s on SVG, 12% faster; 142 vs 148 MiB/s on Maven POM, ~4% slower; 139 vs 157 MiB/s on XHTML, ~13% slower; 169 vs 175 MiB/s on 374KB doc, ~3% slower); serialization 1.5-2.4x faster; XPath evaluation 1.1-2.7x faster (attribute predicates up to 2.7x)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust reimplementation described by its author as 'agent-made' (AI-assisted); not a full libxml2 API-compatible drop-in (has its own MIGRATION.md); benchmark code exists (benches/comparison_bench.rs) but results are mixed, with parsing sometimes slower than libxml2 despite faster serialization and XPath
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or compiler flags disclosed in README for the published numbers; self-reported by the project; parsing throughput wins are inconsistent (4 of 5 tested docs parse at or below libxml2 speed)
